scientists.intro: Dr. Sarah Chen joined for the physics and stayed because leaving would mean admitting the Sphere scares her. Brilliant, curious, sleeping four hours a night. Her notebook margins are full of sketches of the artifact with a face. She denies this.

reactions.minor: Chen logs the incident flatly, then stays three hours late re-running the calibration. 'It wasn't the equipment,' she says, to no one.
reactions.moderate: Chen goes quiet for a day. When she returns, her safety margins are doubled and her eyes are not.
reactions.major: Chen requested reassignment after this one. The request is still sitting on the director's desk, unsigned. She knows. She keeps working.

scientists.intro: Dr. Marcus Reed has survived three lab fires, one flood, and a postdoc under a Nobel tyrant. He treats every anomaly as a personal insult and every injury as paperwork. The staff would follow him into the aperture. He pretends not to know that.

reactions.minor: Reed files the report before the bleeding stops. 'Add it to the list,' he says. There is a list. It is long.
reactions.moderate: Reed takes the night shift himself after this one. Says the junior staff need rest. The truth is he needs to watch the artifact, to make sure it doesn't try anything.
reactions.major: Reed laughed when it happened — one short bark — and then worked a double. The laugh worried everyone more than the incident.

scientists.intro: Dr. Elena Vasquez hears things in the data nobody else hears, which is an asset until it isn't. She named the Choir Glass harmonics before analysis confirmed them. Nobody has asked how. Nobody wants to ask how.

reactions.minor: Vasquez says she expected it. Nobody asks what 'it' was. The log records the incident and, separately, that Vasquez is never wrong about these things.
reactions.moderate: Vasquez stopped humming after this one, and the lab only noticed when the silence got loud. She started again yesterday. Deliberately. Defiantly.
reactions.major: Vasquez looked at the artifact for a long time after this one, the way you look at someone who has hurt you and might do it again. Then she went back to work. There is nothing else to do.

scientists.intro: Dr. Ingrid Lund came from Northwind with her billing honest and her cryogenics colder. She publishes everything, including the things the lab wishes she wouldn't. The artifacts, she insists, deserve accurate footnotes.

reactions.minor: Lund writes up the incident the same day, methods section first. 'If we cannot describe it precisely,' she says, 'we do not understand it at all.'
reactions.moderate: Lund requested the raw data, all of it, and read it twice. Her report is nineteen pages. The conclusion is one sentence long and nobody likes it.
reactions.major: Lund sat with the injured until the medics came, then finished the experiment log before going home. Northwind trained her honestly: the work first, the grief on your own time.

scientists.intro: Dr. Kwame Osei left HELIOS over safety margins and has the resignation letter framed as a reminder. Brilliant on field theory, immovable on procedure. He checks the containment seals twice and trusts them never.

reactions.minor: Osei predicted this exact failure mode in a memo last month. The memo is now taped to the incident board. He says nothing. He does not need to.
reactions.moderate: Osei ran the safety drill nobody else wanted to run, then ran it again. 'HELIOS taught me what happens,' he says, 'when nobody runs it twice.'
reactions.major: Osei went pale and then furious, in that order. This is what he left HELIOS over. He stayed at the bench until the room was certified safe, and only then allowed himself to shake.

scientists.intro: Dr. Anya Petrova contracted for Vantage and knows exactly what wildcards do to people. Fast hands, faster instincts, a past she bills by the hour and never discusses. The artifacts do not surprise her. People do, constantly.

reactions.minor: Petrova had already moved away from the bench before the alarm finished. 'Vantage rule one,' she says. 'Never stand where the money is.'
reactions.moderate: Petrova laughed, once, without humor. She has seen this shape of disaster before, with a different logo on it. Then she got to work like a professional.
reactions.major: Petrova went very still, the way people do when something matches a memory. She will not say which memory. She worked the rest of the shift without a break and billed it all.
